entry.dc:title: EFFECT OF SURFACE MINING ON STORM FLOW AND PEAK FLOW FROM SIX SMALL BASINS IN EASTERN KENTUCKY
entry.dc:creator: Bryan B.
entry.prism:publicationName: Jawra Journal of the American Water Resources Association
entry.dc:description: ABSTRACT: Hydrologic records from six small Eastern Kentucky watersheds were analyzed to determine the effect of surface mining on storm flows and peak flows. Average storm flow volumes were not changed by surface mining, whereas average peak flows were increased 36 percent. Peak flow increases were only in the summer. Smaller peak flows are doubled; moderate ones are increased by about a third; peak flows around 100 csm seem to be largely unaffected; and the larger peak flows may have been reduced by surface mining. The maximum annual storm flows, usually in winter or spring, appeared slightly reduced. No time trend in either storm flows or peak flows could be detected in five years of postmining record. Surface mining is not a serious floodwater discharge problem. Copyright © 1981, Wiley Blackwell. All rights reserved

entry.dc:title: LABORATORY INVESTIGATION OF HYDRAULIC FRACTURING IN OIL SANDS.
entry.dc:creator: Raisbeck J.
entry.dc:description: The design of hydraulic fracturing operations in conjunction with in-situ heavy oil recovery relies on a detailed knowledge of the engineering geology. Although some geotechnical data are available for oil sand deposits in the surface mining area of Athabasca, Alberta (Canada), virtually no information has been published for deeper deposits. The paper reviews the significant physical properties and reports the results from laboratory measurements conducted on oil sands. Data suggest that oil sand may exhibit time-dependent properties under in-situ recovery conditions. The authors also describe exploratory experimentation designed to study conditions under which an open path of fluid injection may be created in oil-sand aggregates.

entry.dc:title: Impact of road building, urbanisation and general infrastructural development on the Nigerian rainforest ecosystem
entry.dc:creator: Ofomata G.
entry.dc:description: Man has increasingly affected the succession of the rainforest ecosystem in Nigeria through various activities connected with his settlement on land. Consequently, little of the Nigerian rainforest ecosystem has remained undisturbed, and extensive areas of original climax vegetation no longer exist in the country. The paper reviews some of the major areas of man's impact on this forest ecosystem. Specifically, it examines me issues of pollution, surface mining, road building, industrialisation and urbanisation. Brief attention is paid to cultural eutrophication, which has been attributed largely to the increase of nitrates and phosphorus added to the water from many sources; this is particularly noticeable in the aquatic sectors of the Nigerian forest ecosystem. Surface mining in Nigeria (which is essentially area strip-mining) causes dereliction of the land, and to combat its undesirable effects, it is suggested that extensive reclamation regulations should be formulated and enforced to cover such issues as slope reduction, back-filling, levelling, revegetation and burying of toxic materials. Industrialisation and urbanisation involve total forest removal, the consequences of which include flooding and soil erosion. Similar consequences arise from road building in the country, and the paper stresses the need to make these operations more rational, not by discontinuing the work but by modifying it so as to save the Nigerian rainforests from total destruction. Accordingly, careful management of the forests is required, whilst continuing the attempt to improve the status of the population. To achieve this desired objective, the paper emphasises the need for a comprehensive national land-use policy, including careful management of the forests. Such an approach would ensure that Nigeria does not indulge in the costly option of improving the circumstances of one generation at the expense of the next. © 1981.

entry.dc:title: Small watershed modeling using DTM.
entry.dc:creator: Eli R.
entry.prism:publicationName: In Water Forum 81 Proc Specialty Conf San Francisco U S A Aug 10 14 1981
entry.prism:volume: II, New York, U.S.A., Am. Soc. Civ. Engrs., 1981
entry.dc:description: Modelling stream flow from small ungauged watersheds is difficult at best, and the difficulties are compounded if watershed characteristics are highly modified by surface mining. In the Eastern United States, the Appalachian coal fields are located in rough terrain and the topography is of major influence. Under these conditions, traditional runoff models using synthesized unit hydrographs are inadequate to determine the hydrologic impacts. Digital terrain modelling (DTM) technology using the ADAPT system is combined with the Hewlett concept of variable source areas of runoff in a proposed concept of continuous or storm event modelling involving the prediction of runoff and sediment yield. (A)

entry.dc:title: Soil-algal relationships from surface mined soils
entry.dc:creator: Shubert L.E.
entry.dc:description: Intensive energy development is taking place in the western United States, because of the large coal reserves that are readily available by surface mining. This study provided baseline data on the physical, chemical and biological properties of spoil and topsoil collected from surface mined sites in three states (Arizona, New Mexico and North Dakota). Integration of analytical data on the physical-chemical properties of the soils with the algae present revealed distinct relationships by the cluster analysis and multiple linear regression methods. High sodium and low nitrogen levels may have accounted for predominance of blue-green algae at the Arizona and New Mexico sites. Other nutrients, such as calcium, chloride and certain trace elements may have been important to the soil algal community. The importance of algae in succession and soil genesis is stressed. © Taylor & Francis Group LLC.

entry.dc:creator: Gunnett J.W.
entry.dc:description: The Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act of 1977, Section 522, establishes requirements for state regulatory authorities to designate lands unsuitable for all or certain types of surface coal mining.
